claim: Reverse replay of hippocampal place cells occurs frequently at rewarded locations.
source: Reverse replay of hippocampal place cells occurs frequently at rewarded locations, suggesting its contribution to goal-directed path learning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation that motivates the study.

claim: Symmetric spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) in CA3 likely potentiates recurrent synapses for both forward and reverse replays during sequential activation of place cells.
source: Symmetric spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) in CA3 likely potentiates recurrent synapses for both forward (start to goal) and reverse (goal to start) replays during sequential activation of place cells.
evidence: This is stated as a premise based on the symmetric nature of STDP in CA3.

claim: Firing sequences bias synaptic transmissions to the opposite direction of propagation under symmetric STDP in the co-presence of short-term synaptic depression or afterdepolarization.
source: Here, we show computationally that firing sequences bias synaptic transmissions to the opposite direction of propagation under symmetric STDP in the co-presence of short-term synaptic depression or afterdepolarization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the computational study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Significant biases are created in biologically realistic simulation settings.
source: We demonstrate that significant biases are created in biologically realistic simulation settings, and this bias enables reverse replay to enhance goal-directed spatial memory on a W-maze.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in the Results section.

claim: The bias mechanism enables reverse replay to enhance goal-directed spatial memory on a W-maze.
source: We demonstrate that significant biases are created in biologically realistic simulation settings, and this bias enables reverse replay to enhance goal-directed spatial memory on a W-maze.
evidence: This is demonstrated through W-maze simulations in Figure 7 and Figure 8.

claim: The same mechanism works in a two-dimensional open field.
source: Further, we show that essentially the same mechanism works in a two-dimensional open field.
evidence: This is demonstrated through 2D open field simulations in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: The hippocampus plays an important role in episodic memory and spatial processing in the brain.
source: The hippocampus plays an important role in episodic memory and spatial processing in the brain (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Scoville and Milner, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: Firing sequences of place cells are replayed during awake immobility and sleep.
source: In the rodent hippocampus, firing sequences of place cells are replayed during awake immobility and sleep (Carr et al., 2011; Pfeiffer, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Reactivations of place cell sequences are crucial for performance in spatial memory tasks.
source: and these reactivations are crucial for performance in spatial memory tasks (Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012; Singer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies showing disruption of replay impairs memory.

claim: Forward replay is observed during sleep after exploration or in immobile states before rats start to travel towards reward.
source: Forward replay is observed during sleep after exploration (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2013) or in immobile states before rats start to travel towards reward (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Forward replay is thought to engage in the consolidation and retrieval of spatial memory.
source: hence forward replay is thought to engage in the consolidation and retrieval of spatial memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing and context of forward replay observations.

claim: Reverse replay presumably contributes to the optimization of goal-directed paths because rewarded spatial paths are replayed around the timing of reward delivery.
source: In contrast, reverse replay presumably contributes to the optimization of goal-directed paths because rewarded spatial paths are replayed around the timing of reward delivery (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006)
evidence: This is an inference supported by experimental observations of reverse replay timing.

claim: The occurrence frequency of reverse replay is modulated by the presence and the amount of reward.
source: and the occurrence frequency is modulated by the presence and the amount of reward (Ambrose et al., 2016; Singer and Frank, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Asymmetric STDP found in CA1 induces long-term potentiation (LTP) for pre-to-post firing order and long-term depression (LTD) for post-to-pre firing order.
source: Because sequences are essentially time asymmetric, sequence learning often hypothesizes asymmetric spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) found in CA1 (Bi and Poo , 2001) which induce long-term potentiation (LTP) for pre-to-post firing order and long-term depression (LTD) for post-to-pre firing order.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental characterization of STDP in CA1.

claim: Asymmetric STDP enables a recurrent network to reactivate sequential firing in the same order with the experience.
source: This type of STDP enables a recurrent network to reactivate sequential firing in the same order with the experience.
evidence: This is a well-established theoretical result in computational neuroscience.

claim: The default form of STDP is time symmetric at recurrent synapses in hippocampal area CA3.
source: However, in the hippocampal area CA3, it was recently reported that the default form of STDP is time symmetric at recurrent synapses (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: CA3 is the most likely source of hippocampal firing sequences.
source: Because CA3 is the most likely source of hippocampal firing sequences (Middleton and McHugh, 2016; Nakashiba et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: A symmetric time window implies that a firing sequence equally strengthens both forward and reverse synaptic pathways in CA3 recurrent network.
source: A symmetric time window implies that a firing sequence equally strengthens both forward synaptic pathways leading to the rewarded location and reverse pathways leaving away from the rewarded location in CA3 recurrent network.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the symmetric nature of the STDP rule.

claim: Reward-based optimization requires selective reinforcement of forward pathways.
source: However, reward-based optimization requires selective reinforcement of forward pathways as it will strengthen prospective place-cell sequences in subsequent trials and forward replay events in the consolidation phase.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for goal-directed learning.

claim: Bias toward forward sequences in post-experience sleep is observed in hippocampus.
source: Such bias toward forward sequences in post-experience sleep (Wikenheiser and Redish, 2013) and goal-directed behavior (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015) is actually observed in hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The contribution of presynaptic spiking for STDP is attenuated in CA3 by short-term depression, as was revealed in the rat visual cortex.
source: To this end, we hypothesize that the contribution of presynaptic spiking for STDP is attenuated in CA3 by short-term depression, as was revealed in the rat visual cortex (Froemke et al., 2006).
evidence: This hypothesis is based on experimental findings in visual cortex, extended to CA3.

claim: Under the condition of STP-modulated symmetric STDP, the combined rule virtually acts like anti-Hebbian STDP.
source: Under this condition, symmetric STDP and a rate-based Hebbian plasticity rule bias recurrent synaptic weights toward the opposite direction to the propagation of a firing sequence, implying that the combined rule virtually acts like anti-Hebbian STDP.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Accumulation of afterdepolarization in postsynaptic neurons results in the same effect as STP modulation.
source: We also show that accumulation of afterdepolarization (Mishra et al., 2016) in postsynaptic neurons results in the same effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Standard Hebbian plasticity rule potentiated excitatory synaptic weights symmetrically without creating any bias during unidirectional sequence propagation.
source: During the propagation of the first unidirectional sequence, this rule potentiated synaptic weights symmetrically without creating any bias in the synaptic weights (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: When synaptic weights were changed by a modified Hebbian plasticity rule modulated by STP, the second firing sequence only propagated to the reverse direction of the first one.
source: However, when synaptic weights were changed by a modified Hebbian plasticity rule (see Materials and methods), in which the long-term plasticity is also regulated by STP at presynaptic terminals (Froemke et al., 2006), the second firing sequence only propagated to the reverse direction of the first one (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The first firing sequence potentiated synaptic weights asymmetrically in the forward and reverse directions, creating a bias in the spatial distribution of synaptic weights.
source: This selective propagation occurred because the first firing sequence potentiated synaptic weights asymmetrically in the forward and reverse directions, thus creating a bias in the spatial distribution of synaptic weights (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neurotransmitters are exhausted in the tail of the activity packet, so presynaptic outputs are effective only at the head of the activity packet.
source: Because neurotransmitters are exhausted in the tail of the activity packet, presynaptic outputs are effective only at the head of the activity packet.
evidence: This is explained based on the STP dynamics shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Due to spatial asymmetricity of presynaptic outputs, connections from the head to the tail are strongly potentiated but those from the tail to the head are not.
source: Due to this spatial asymmetricity of presynaptic outputs, connections from the head to the tail are strongly potentiated but those from the tail to the head are not (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1F and explained mechanistically.

claim: The packet of presynaptic outputs becomes somewhat 'prospective' (slightly skewed toward the direction of activity propagation).
source: In other words, the packet of presynaptic outputs becomes somewhat 'prospective' (namely, slightly skewed toward the direction of activity propagation)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Weight changes based on coincidences between presynaptic outputs and postsynaptic activities result in selective potentiation of connections from the 'future' to the 'past' in the firing sequence.
source: so the weight changes based on the coincidences between presynaptic outputs and postsynaptic activities result in the selective potentiation of connections from the 'future' to the 'past' in the firing sequence.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation of the simulation results.

claim: This mechanism was not known previously and enables forward sequences to potentiate the synaptic transmissions responsible for reverse replay, and vice versa.
source: This mechanism was not known previously and enables forward sequences to potentiate the synaptic transmissions responsible for reverse replay, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and implications of the finding.

claim: Similar asymmetricity and potentiation of reverse synaptic transmission can emerge when the effect of postsynaptic activity on Hebbian plasticity accumulates through time.
source: Meanwhile, similar asymmetricity, and hence the potentiation of reverse synaptic transmission, can also emerge when the effect of postsynaptic activity on Hebbian plasticity accumulates through time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: STDP in CA3 depends on the afterdepolarization (ADP) in dendrites.
source: Because STDP in CA3 depends on the afterdepolarization (ADP) in dendrites (Mishra et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The ADP-dependent phenomenon will occur if the effect of ADPs accumulates over multiple postsynaptic spikes as afterhyperpolarization modulates STDP in the visual cortex.
source: this phenomenon will occur if the effect of ADPs accumulates over multiples postsynaptic spikes as afterhyperpolarization modulates STDP in the visual cortex (Froemke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on analogy to visual cortex findings.

claim: Symmetric STDP modulated by STP biased the weight changes to the reverse direction in spiking neuron networks.
source: However, symmetric STDP modulated by STP biased the weight changes to the reverse direction (Figure 2C), and accordingly the second firing sequence selectively traveled towards the opposite direction to the first sequence (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The effect of STP-modulated symmetric STDP did not depend significantly on synaptic time constants.
source: This effect did not depend significantly on synaptic time constants, and we could obtain the same effect when we turned off NMDA current and shortened time constants for AMPA and inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Under asymmetric STDP without modulation by STP, firing sequences strengthened the forward sequence propagation.
source: In contrast, under asymmetric STDP without modulation by STP, firing sequences strengthened the forward sequence propagation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and the related synaptic connections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), as expected.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Introducing modulation by STP did not change the qualitative results for asymmetric STDP.
source: Introducing modulation by STP did not change the qualitative results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: A greater potentiation of reverse synaptic transmissions in CA3 occurs under the modified symmetric STDP.
source: These results indicate that a greater potentiation of reverse synaptic transmissions in CA3 occurs under the modified symmetric STDP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spiking neuron simulations.

claim: Significant biases toward the reverse direction were observed in broad simulation conditions with Poisson spike trains.
source: Significant biases toward the reverse direction were observed in broad simulation conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: The biases were statistically significant already in a part of conditions with two spikes per neuron, and the effect became prominent as the number of spikes increased.
source: The biases were statistically significant (p<0.01 in Wilcoxon signed rank test for mean bias or binomial test for P(bias >0)) already in a part of conditions with two spikes per neuron, and the effect became prominent as the number of spikes increased.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with statistical tests.

claim: The magnitude of synaptic changes is larger for a faster spike propagation.
source: In general, the magnitude of synaptic changes is larger for a faster spike propagation (Figure 3D, Table 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Table 1 with correlation analysis.

claim: P(bias >0) was greater for a smaller mean ISI, and it did not depend on the propagation speed.
source: On the other hand, P(bias >0) was greater for a smaller mean ISI, and it did not depend on the propagation speed (Figure 3D, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Table 1 with correlation analysis.

claim: All simulations showed statistically significant biases to the reverse direction when the number of spikes per neuron is 4 or five and the mean ISI <20 ms, regardless of propagation speed.
source: Especially, all simulations showed statistically significant biases to the reverse direction regardless of the propagation speed when the number of spikes per neuron is 4 or five and the mean ISI <20 ms.
evidence: This is stated based on the results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The bias toward the reverse direction is most prominent when the neural network propagates a sequence of bursts with intraburst ISIs less than 20 ms.
source: This implies that the bias toward the reverse direction is the most prominent when the neural network propagates a sequence of bursts with intraburst ISIs less than 20 ms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Bursting is observed in CA3 in vivo.
source: Such bursting is actually observed in CA3 in vivo (Mizuseki et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Simulations of a CA3 recurrent network model suggest that bursting plays a crucial role in propagation of firing sequences.
source: and simulations of a CA3 recurrent network model suggest that bursting plays a crucial role in propagation of firing sequences (Omura et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: Both mean bias and P(bias>0) clearly depend on the initial release probability.
source: As shown in Figure 4 and Table 1, both mean bias and P(bias>0) clearly depend on the initial release probability.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The bias toward the reverse direction occurred robustly for a sufficiently high intraburst firing frequency and a sufficiently high release probability of neurotransmitters.
source: In sum, the bias toward the reverse direction occurred robustly for a sufficiently high intraburst firing frequency and a sufficiently high release probability of neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the Poisson spike train simulations.

claim: Asymmetric STDP was not effective in potentiating reversed synaptic transmissions even if it was modulated by STP.
source: In contrast to symmetric STDP, asymmetric STDP was not effective in potentiating reversed synaptic transmissions even if it was modulated by STP.
evidence: This is stated based on simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Asymmetric STDP with all-to-all spike coupling never generated potentiation of reverse transmissions for any parameter value of STP and the number of spikes per neuron.
source: In our simulations with parameters taken from experiments in CA1 (Bi and Poo , 2001), such a potentiation effect was never observed for asymmetric STDP with all-to-all spike coupling for any parameter value of STP and the number of spikes per neuron (5 or 15 spikes) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Asymmetric STDP with nearest-neighbor spike coupling generated statistically significant biases toward the reverse direction in some parameter region.
source: However, asymmetric STDP with nearest-neighbor spike coupling (Izhikevich and Desai, 2003a), in which only the nearest postsynaptic spikes before and after a presynaptic spike were taken into account, generated statistically significant biases toward the reverse direction in some parameter region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a rat passes through place fields of CA3 place cells, they typically show bell-shape activity patterns with duration of about 1 s and mean peak firing rate of about 13 Hz.
source: When a rat passes through place fields of CA3 place cells, they typically shows bell-shape activity patterns duration of which is about 1 s and mean peak firing rate is about 13 Hz (Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013; Mizuseki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Firing of place cells is phase-locked to theta oscillation and the firing phase gradually advances as a rat moves through place fields (theta-phase precession).
source: Firing of place cells is phase-locked to theta oscillation and the firing phase gradually advances as a rat moves through place fields (theta-phase precession).
evidence: This is a well-known phenomenon in hippocampal physiology.

claim: Firing sequences of place cells scan the path from behind to ahead of the rat in every theta cycle, which is a phenomenon called theta sequence.
source: Furthermore, firing sequences of place cells scan the path from behind to ahead of the rat in every theta cycle, which is a phenomenon called theta sequence (Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007; Huxter et al., 2008; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Wang et al., 2015; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Weight biases primarily depended on coarse-grained firing rates, but phase selectivity had no significant effect in the model.
source: We found that weight biases primarily depended on coarse-grained firing rates, but phase selectivity had no significant effect in our model (Figure 5B, Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: Noticeable effects of phase selectivity on weight biases emerged for a narrow STDP time window of 10 ms.
source: Noticeable effects of phase selectivity on weight biases emerged for a narrow STDP time window of 10 ms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: Experimentally observed broad time window of STDP (70 ms) masks small differences in firing phases.
source: suggesting that experimentally observed broad time window of STDP (70 ms) masks small differences in firing phases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results comparing narrow and broad STDP windows.

claim: 13 Hz mean peak firing rate was not high enough to induce statistically significant bias in simulations of place cell activity during run.
source: As for the mean peak firing rate, 13 Hz was not high enough to induce statistically significant bias in these simulations.
evidence: This is stated based on the results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The summation of synaptic inputs from ten place cells with identical place fields amplified weight biases, and the bias became significant at 13 Hz.
source: First, the summation of synaptic inputs from ten place cells with identical (or overlapped) place fields amplified weight biases, and the bias became significant at 13 Hz in this case (Figure 5C, Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and Table 2.

claim: Firing rates of place cells obey a log-normal distribution and a small fraction of place cells exhibits extremely high firing rates (>30 Hz).
source: Second, firing rates of place cells obey a log-normal distribution and a small fraction of place cells exhibits extremely high firing rates (>30 Hz) (Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Place cells with extremely high firing rates created large weight changes and significant directional biases.
source: These cells created large weight changes and significant directional biases (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The bias effect in the model is weaker during run than in replay events because mean firing rate is lower and theta phase-locking is not effective for learning with broad symmetric STDP.
source: Taken together, the bias effect in our model is weaker during run than in replay events because mean firing rate is lower and theta phase-locking is not effective for learning with broad symmetric STDP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulations of run and replay.

claim: Enhanced firing propagation by STP and relatively slow long-term plasticity are necessary to create strongly biased forward synaptic pathways through reverse replay.
source: These results demonstrate that enhanced firing propagation by STP and relatively slow long-term plasticity are necessary to create strongly biased forward synaptic pathways through reverse replay.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: After a few traversals on the W-maze, the network generated reverse replay at D1 and D2 and forward replay at A during immobility.
source: After a few traversals on the W-maze, the network generated reverse replay at D1 and D2 (Figure 7D and E, red arrows) and forward replay at A (Figure 7D and E, black arrows) during immobility
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: In trial five and later trials, forward replay selectively traveled towards the rewarded position D2.
source: Notably, in trial five and later trials, forward replay selectively traveled towards the rewarded position D2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Firing sequences that started from the non-rewarded position D1 propagated to the rewarded position D2 but not to the start A.
source: Furthermore, firing sequences that started from the non-rewarded position D1 propagated to the rewarded position D2 but not to the start A (Figure 7D and E, blue arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The network model could combine multiple spatial paths to form a synaptic pathway that has not been traversed by the animal.
source: Thus, the network model could combine multiple spatial paths to form a synaptic pathway that has not been traversed by the animal.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that sequences propagated from D1 to D2 without the animal experiencing this path.

claim: After exploration on the W-maze, the connection vector field was organized so as to route neural activities to those neurons encoding the rewarded position on the track.
source: However, after the exploration, the vector field was organized so as to route neural activities to those neurons encoding the rewarded position on the track (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A similar route map was obtained when the sequential order of visits to the two arms was reversed.
source: A similar route map was also obtained when we reversed the sequential order of visits to the two arms (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The route map was abolished when reward was removed.
source: but was abolished when we removed reward (Figure 8—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: The route map was abolished when the effect of STP on Hebbian plasticity was removed.
source: or the effect of STP on Hebbian plasticity (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: Direct synaptic pathways from D1 to D2 were created through the learning mechanism.
source: As demonstrated previously, direct synaptic pathways from D1 to D2 were also created.
evidence: This is stated based on the results shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Connections are biased from goal to start when there is no reward at the goal because theta sequences enhance synaptic pathways opposite to the direction of animal's movement.
source: First, as seen in Figure 8—figure supplement 3, connections are biased from goal to start when there is no reward at the goal because theta sequences enhance synaptic pathways opposite to the direction of animal's movement.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3 and explained mechanistically.

claim: In non-rewarded travels, directional biases are not overwritten by reverse replay.
source: In non-rewarded travels, these directional biases are not overwritten by reverse replay.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the absence of reward-triggered reverse replay.

claim: The relative preference of a synaptic pathway in hippocampal sequential firing decreases for exploration that does not result in reward.
source: Thus, the relative preference of a synaptic pathway in hippocampal sequential firing decreases for exploration that does not result in reward.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Some reverse replay sequences from D2 propagate into D1 instead of the stem arm, and such joint replay enhances biases towards goal through unexperienced spatial paths.
source: Second, some of reverse replay sequences from D2 propagates into D1 instead of the stem arm (Figure 7E and G and Figure 7—video 1), and such joint replay enhances biases towards goal through unexperienced spatial paths.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E, 7G and video 1.

claim: The model creates a map not only for the spatial paths experienced by the animal, but also for their possible combinations if they guide the animal directly to the rewarded position.
source: Thus, our model creates a map not only for the spatial paths experienced by the animal, but also for their possible combinations if they guide the animal directly to the rewarded position from a point in the space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the W-maze simulations.

claim: The model optimizes the cognitive map of the spatial environment.
source: In this sense, our model optimizes the cognitive map of the spatial environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's function.

claim: When theta oscillation was turned off, the network model generated replay-like long-lasting firing sequences not only during immobility, but also during run.
source: When we turned off theta oscillation, the network model generated replay-like long-lasting firing sequences not only during immobility, but also during run (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Theta oscillation offers periodic hyperpolarization of the membrane potentials that terminates firing sequences in a short period and localizes place-cell activity.
source: In our model, theta oscillation offers periodic hyperpolarization of the membrane potentials that terminates firing sequences in a short period and localizes place-cell activity.
evidence: This is an explanation of the role of theta oscillation in the model.

claim: Firing sequences triggered at reward sites propagate isotropically from trigger points in a 2-D space, rather than as reverse replay of recent paths.
source: These observations suggest that firing sequences during immobility in a 2-D space propagate isotropically from trigger points, rather than reverse replay of recent paths.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations cited in the text.

claim: The model predicts that firing sequences triggered at reward sites are beneficial for goal-directed path learning in a 2-D space.
source: Our model predicts that such firing sequences triggered at reward sites are beneficial for goal-directed path learning in a 2-D space.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model's mechanism.

claim: Divergent firing sequences from the center created a connection vector field converging to the center.
source: Because sequence propagation potentiates synaptic pathways in the opposite direction, these divergent firing sequences created the connection vector field converging to the center (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Isotropic sequence propagation from reward sites achieves goal-directed sequence learning in a 2-D (or even 3-D) open field.
source: This result generalizes the role of 1-D reverse replay to higher dimensional spaces: isotropic sequence propagation from reward sites achieves goal-directed sequence learning in a 2-D (or even 3-D) open field.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2-D simulation results.

claim: The model quickly learned efficient goal-directed navigation after every SWITCH trial in the 2-D foraging task.
source: The model quickly learned efficient goal-directed navigation after every SWITCH trial (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The bias at the goal was almost zero, the same level as a random search.
source: The bias at the goal was almost zero, that is, the same level as a random search.
evidence: This is stated based on the results shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The bias from start to goal was stronger than that from goal to recent paths (reverse replay) in REPEAT trials, which is consistent with experimental observation.
source: These results suggest that the bias from start to goal was stronger than that from goal to recent paths (reverse replay) in REPEAT trials, which is consistent with experimental observation (Pfeiffer, 2018; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results that is consistent with cited experiments.

claim: Weight biases affected propagation of theta sequences during exploration.
source: Furthermore, the bias during exploration suggests that weight biases also affected propagation of theta sequences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bias observed during the run period.

claim: The bias to recent paths in SWITCH trials can be explained by the fact that the animal typically reached reward after visiting the previous reward site which strongly attracted firing sequences.
source: This bias to recent paths in SWITCH trials can be explained by the fact that the animal typically reached reward after visiting the previous reward site which strongly attracted firing sequences (Figure 10E and F).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the simulation results shown in Figure 10E and F.

claim: The bias to recent paths gives an efficient way to update connection weights for the new reward site because updating weight biases is unnecessary outside the space between the goals.
source: Notably, this bias gives an efficient way to update connection weights for the new reward site because the connection vector fields converging to the two goals differ only in the space between the goals and updating weight biases is unnecessary outside this space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational efficiency of the learning mechanism.

claim: The model predicts that the bias of sequence propagation from a novel goal position to previously learned goals appears when the animal should update previous memories to a new memory.
source: Thus, our model predicts that the bias of sequence propagation from a novel goal position to previously learned goals appears when the animal should update previous memories to a new memory.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: Divergent sequences create weight biases for convergent sequence propagation to goals in the model and this learning mechanism can be a basis for efficient goal-directed navigation in the 2-D space.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that divergent sequences create weight biases for convergent sequence propagation to goals in our model and this learning mechanism can be a basis for efficient goal-directed navigation in the 2-D space.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the 2-D foraging simulations.

claim: The modified Hebbian plasticity rule modulated by STP biases synaptic weights toward the reverse direction of the firing sequences that traveled through a recurrent network.
source: In this paper, we showed that the modified Hebbian plasticity rule modulated by STP biases synaptic weights toward the reverse direction of the firing sequences that traveled through a recurrent network.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The phenomenon favors spike bursts and a high presynaptic release probability.
source: We further clarified for various Poisson-like sequential firing patterns that the phenomenon favors spike bursts and a high presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The selective potentiation of reverse directions is unlikely to occur for the conventional asymmetric STDP.
source: We also showed that the selective potentiation of reverse directions is unlikely to occur for the conventional asymmetric STDP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reverse replay is crucial for the reinforcement of reward-seeking behavior in the animal.
source: Because the frequency of reverse replay increases at rewarded positions (Ambrose et al., 2016; Singer and Frank, 2009), reward delivery induces the preferential potentiation of forward synaptic pathways, which in turn results in an enhanced occurrence of forward replay in the consolidation phase. Thus, our model predicts that reverse replay is crucial for the reinforcement of reward-seeking behavior in the animal
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model's mechanism and cited experimental observations.

claim: The model provides the mechanistic account for the way reverse replay enables the hippocampal prospective coding of reward-seeking navigation.
source: and gives, for the first time, the mechanistic account for the way reverse replay enables the hippocampal prospective coding of reward-seeking navigation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and contribution of the model.

claim: If the occurrence of reverse replay is modulated by other salient events, the model is immediately generalized to memorization of important paths to be replayed afterwards.
source: Furthermore, if the occurrence of reverse replay is modulated not only by reward but also by other salient events for the animal, this model is immediately generalized to memorization of important paths to be replayed afterwards.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the model.

claim: The model reinforces unexperienced spatial paths by connecting multiple paths that were previously encoded by separate experiences.
source: Importantly, our model reinforces unexperienced spatial paths by connecting the multiple paths that were previously encoded by separate experiences.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the W-maze simulations.

claim: The hippocampus can generate replay along joint paths even when the animal has no direct experience.
source: The hippocampus can generate replay along joint paths (Wu and Foster, 2014) even when the animal has no direct experience (Gupta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The model shows that reverse replay creates a bias to the forward direction even in the very early stage of learning.
source: In 1-D tracks, reverse replay is observed immediately after the first lap (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Wu and Foster, 2014). Our model shows that such a replay creates a bias to the forward direction (i.e. toward the reward) even in the very early stage of learning.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model's mechanism and cited experimental observations.

claim: A weak bias to forward replay was observed in the first exposure to a long 1-D track.
source: Consistently, a weak bias to forward replay was observed in the first exposure to a long 1-D track (Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: The model predicts that the bias to the goal-directed sequences will be suppressed (or enhanced) if we selectively block (or enhance) reverse replay at the goal.
source: Our model predicts that the bias to the goal-directed sequences will be suppressed (or enhanced) if we selectively block (or enhance) reverse replay at the goal.
evidence: This is a testable prediction based on the model's mechanism.

claim: The most critical assumption in the model is the rapid modulation of STDP coherent to the presynaptic neurotransmitter release of STP.
source: The most critical assumption in our model is the rapid modulation of STDP coherent to the presynaptic neurotransmitter release of STP.
evidence: This is stated as a key assumption of the model.

claim: Such a modulation of STDP by STP was reported in the visual cortex.
source: Such a modulation was actually reported in the visual cortex (Froemke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: Short-term depression exists in CA3.
source: Although short-term depression also exists in CA3 (Guzman et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: STDP is modulated in a slightly different fashion in the hippocampus: the strong modulation arises from the second presynaptic spike rather than the first one.
source: STDP is modulated in a slightly different fashion in the hippocampus: the strong modulation arises from the second presynaptic spike rather than the first one (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: The experiment on STDP modulation was performed in a dissociated culture in which hippocampal sub-regions were not distinguished.
source: However, the experiment was performed in a dissociated culture in which hippocampal sub-regions were not distinguished.
evidence: This is a caveat about the cited experimental study.

claim: The modulation of STDP was not tested for more than two presynaptic spikes, and whether a third presynaptic spike further facilitates or rather depresses STDP remains unknown.
source: Moreover, the modulation of STDP was not tested for more than two presynaptic spikes, and whether a third presynaptic spike further facilitates or rather depresses STDP remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing experimental data.

claim: The contributions of STP to STDP should be further validated in CA3.
source: Therefore, the contributions of STP to STDP should be further validated in CA3.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future experimental work.

claim: The proposed role of short-term depression in biasing replay events may be examined by pharmacological blockade or enhancement of STP in the hippocampus.
source: The proposed role of short-term depression in biasing replay events may also be examined by pharmacological blockade or enhancement of STP in the hippocampus (Froemke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental testing of the model.

claim: The dendritic ADP accumulated over multiple spikes can be directly tested in CA3 by modifying the protocol described previously.
source: In addition, we showed that the dendritic ADP accumulated over multiple spikes causes a similar phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This can be directly tested in CA3 by modifying the protocol described previously (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental testing of the model.

claim: CA3 primarily receives dopaminergic input from the locus coeruleus (LC) which signals novelty and facilitate learning in the hippocampus.
source: CA3 primarily receives dopaminergic input from the locus coeruleus (LC) which signals novelty and facilitate learning in the hippocampus (Takeuchi et al., 2016; Wagatsuma et al., 2018; Walling et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Sequence learning in CA3 is affected by novelty and salience of events.
source: Therefore, sequence learning in CA3 is also affected by novelty and salience of events (Lisman and Grace, 2005; Lisman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of LC input and cited theoretical work.

claim: Any place in which the animal experiences behaviorally important events can be a potential goal for the hippocampal path learning.
source: Consequently, any place in which the animal experiences behaviorally important events can be a potential goal for the hippocampal path learning
evidence: This is an inference based on the model's mechanism.

claim: Valence of the goal is encoded in downstream areas.
source: and valence of the goal is encoded in downstream areas (de Lavilléon et al., 2015; Redondo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model may explain sequence learning for fear memory and vicarious trial and error in hippocampus.
source: This may explain sequence learning for fear memory (Wu et al., 2017) and vicarious trial and error in hippocampus, that is, evaluation of potential paths before decision making (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Singer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the model's applicability to other phenomena.

claim: In the model, reverse replay in CA3 contributes to selective forward replay of paths informative for decision making.
source: In this case, reverse replay in CA3 contributes to selective forward replay of paths informative for decision making.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's function in decision-making contexts.

claim: Modulation of triggering replay events crucially affects the learning with reverse replay in the model.
source: In our model, modulation of triggering replay events (or sharp wave ripples) crucially affects the learning with reverse replay.
evidence: This is stated based on the model's mechanism.

claim: The area CA2 encodes the current position during immobility and can trigger sharp wave ripples.
source: The area CA2 encodes the current position during immobility (Kay et al., 2016) and can trigger sharp wave ripples (Oliva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Dopaminergic enhancement in CA2 may increase replay events from the current position.
source: Thus, dopaminergic enhancement in CA2 may increase replay events from the current position as in our simulation settings.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of CA2.

claim: Dentate gyrus intensively encodes reward sites and triggers sharp wave ripples in CA3 in working memory task.
source: Dentate gyrus intensively encodes reward sites and triggers sharp wave ripples in CA3 in working memory task (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: If dentate gyrus-triggered ripples accompany replay sequences, CA2 and dentate gyrus also play active roles in the goal selection of hippocampal path learning.
source: If this is indeed the case, our results suggest that CA2 and dentate gyrus also play active roles in the goal selection of hippocampal path learning.
evidence: This is a conditional prediction based on the model.

claim: The model predicts that the release probability of neurotransmitter strongly affects the magnitude and probability of bias toward the reverse direction.
source: Our model also predicts that the release probability of neurotransmitter strongly affects the magnitude and probability of bias toward the reverse direction (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modulation of neurotransmitter release in CA3 can regulate the behavioral impact of hippocampal firing sequences.
source: Therefore, modulation of neurotransmitter release in CA3 can regulate the behavioral impact of hippocampal firing sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model's mechanism.

claim: Presynaptic long-term plasticity may affect the directional biases at longer timescales.
source: Presynaptic long-term plasticity (Costa et al., 2015) may also affect the directional biases at longer timescales.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential effects of presynaptic LTP.

claim: The strength of theta phase-locking of place cell activity did not have significant effects on learning in the simulation.
source: In our simulation, the strength of theta phase-locking of place cell activity did not have significant effects on learning (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: This result poses a question against the long-standing hypothesis that theta sequences are essential for sequence learning.
source: This result poses a question against the long-standing hypothesis that theta sequences are essential for sequence learning (Jensen and Lisman, 1996; 2005; Sato and Yamaguchi, 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results in relation to previous hypotheses.

claim: It is possible that theta phase-locking is effective in learning CA3-to-CA1 connections at which STDP is asymmetric and more sensitive to time differences.
source: However, it is possible that theta phase-locking is effective in learning CA3-to-CA1 connections at which STDP is asymmetric and more sensitive to time differences between presynaptic and postsynaptic activities than at CA3 recurrent synapses (Bi and Poo , 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation about where theta phase-locking might be important.

claim: Simulations in the 2-D space showed that theta sequences can act as readout of weight biases to reward, and hence are useful for planning future trajectories during exploration.
source: Furthermore, our simulations in the 2-D space showed that theta sequences can act as readout of weight biases to reward, and hence are useful for planning future trajectories during exploration.
evidence: This is shown in the 2-D foraging simulations.

claim: This role of theta sequences is consistent with experimental findings.
source: This role of theta sequences is consistent with experimental findings (Huxter et al., 2008; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Short-term facilitation contributed to the generation of theta sequences.
source: Short-term facilitation also had only limited effects on the proposed learning mechanism (Figure 4); however, it contributed to the generation of theta sequences (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on model results and cited work.

claim: In the model, short-term facilitation enhances the readout of spatial information during run.
source: Therefore, in our model, short-term facilitation also enhances the readout of spatial information during run.
evidence: This is an inference about the role of short-term facilitation in the model.

claim: How the learning mechanism is related to TD learning should be mathematically investigated in the future.
source: Thus, how our learning mechanism is related to TD learning should be mathematically investigated in the future.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future theoretical work.

claim: A conceptual model has been proposed for goal-directed sequence learning with symmetric STDP based on the gradient field of connection strength.
source: A conceptual model has been proposed for goal-directed sequence learning with symmetric STDP based on the gradient field of connection strength (Pfeiffer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous model.

claim: The conceptual model concluded that goal-directed sequence learning would not occur if sequences homogenously propagate through the entire space.
source: The conceptual model concluded that goal-directed sequence learning would not occur if sequences homogenously propagate through the entire space.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusion of the cited conceptual model.

claim: The present model shows that goal-directed learning can occur with homogeneous sequence propagation for STP-modulated symmetric STDP.
source: However, our model shows that this is not the case for STP-modulated symmetric STDP and proposes a network mechanism to implement the conceptual model based on reverse replay.
evidence: This is a claim about how the present model differs from and extends the conceptual model.

claim: The model has yet to be improved to learn context-dependent switching of behavior such as navigation on an alternating T-maze.
source: While the present model could demonstrate goal-directed path learning, the model has yet to be improved to learn context-dependent switching of behavior such as navigation on an alternating T-maze.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current model.

claim: A straightforward extension of the model is to maintain multiple charts representing the alternating paths and switch them according to the stored short-term memory or certain context information.
source: A straightforward extension of our model is to maintain multiple charts representing the alternating paths (Samsonovich and McNaughton, 1997) and switch them according to the stored short-term memory or certain context information.
evidence: This is a suggestion for extending the model.

claim: Each chart will be selectively reinforced by reverse replay along one of the alternating paths.
source: Each chart will be selectively reinforced by reverse replay along one of the alternating paths.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the extended model would work.

claim: This switching of CA3 activity may be supported by the dentate gyrus.
source: This switching of CA3 activity may be supported by the dentate gyrus (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited experimental work.

claim: How to protect the previous memories from overwriting with novel reward experiences is an important issue that is left unsolved by the present model.
source: How to protect the previous memories from overwriting with novel reward experiences is another important issue that is left unsolved by the present model.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current model.

claim: One solution for protecting previous memories is triggering remote replay at the previous reward sites.
source: If the animal can memorize all four candidate reward sites simultaneously, the animal can efficiently search reward even when the reward position is changed in every trial. One solution for this issue is triggering remote replay (Gupta et al., 2010; Karlsson and Frank, 2009) at the previous reward sites.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential solution.

claim: The model predicts that bias of starting points of remote replay affects persistence of multiple memories.
source: Thus, we predict that bias of starting points of remote replay affects persistence of multiple memories.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model's mechanism.

claim: While 2-D hippocampal place cells are omnidirectional, the majority of 1-D place cells are unidirectional.
source: While 2-D hippocampal place cells are omnidirectional, the majority of 1-D place cells are unidirectional (Buzsáki, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: The model did not take into account the unidirectional property of 1-D place cells.
source: We did not take into account this property of 1-D place cells in this study.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the model.

claim: To learn unexperienced paths with unidirectional place cells, continuous replay events of multiple unidirectional place-cell ensembles is necessary, which has been experimentally observed.
source: To learn unexperienced paths, continuous replay events of multiple unidirectional place-cell ensembles is necessary, which has been experimentally observed (Davidson et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2010; Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Neural network models demonstrated that Hebbian plasticity can connect multiple unidirectional place cells at the junction points.
source: Neural network models also demonstrated that Hebbian plasticity can connect multiple unidirectional place cells at the junction points (Brunel and Trullier, 1998; Buzsáki, 2005; Káli and Dayan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Replay of long paths and complex spatial structures is often accompanied by concatenated sharp wave ripples.
source: Relating to this, replay of long paths and complex spatial structures is often accompanied by concatenated sharp wave ripples (Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Each sharp wave ripple corresponds to a segment in the spatial structure.
source: Interestingly, each sharp wave ripple corresponds to a segment in the spatial structure (Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Reverse replay has not been found in the neocortical circuits.
source: Reverse replay has not been found in the neocortical circuits.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of experimental observations.

claim: Firing sequences in the rodent prefrontal cortex are reactivated only in the forward directions.
source: For instance, firing sequences in the rodent prefrontal cortex are reactivated only in the forward directions (Euston et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Neocortical synapses obey asymmetric STDP.
source: To the best of our knowledge, neocortical synapses obey asymmetric STDP (Froemke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: If dopamine turns asymmetric STDP into symmetric STDP in neocortex, forward firing sequences will reinforce the propagation of reverse sequences.
source: However, if dopamine turns asymmetric STDP into symmetric STDP, which is actually the case in hippocampal area CA1 (Brzosko et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009), forward firing sequences will reinforce the propagation of reverse sequences.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known effects of dopamine in CA1.

claim: The proposed neural mechanism of path learning may give a cue for exploring the neural substrate for logic operations by the brain.
source: The proposed neural mechanism of path learning may give a cue for exploring the neural substrate for logic operations by the brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about broader implications of the model.

claim: The model proposes a biologically plausible mechanism for goal-directed path learning through reverse sequences.
source: In sum, our model proposes a biologically plausible mechanism for goal-directed path learning through reverse sequences.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the model's contribution.

claim: In dynamic programming-based path finding methods, a globally optimal path is determined by backtrack from the goal to the start after an exhaustive local search of forward paths.
source: In the dynamic programming-based path finding methods such as Dijkstra's algorithm for finding the shortest path (Dijkstra, 1959) and Viterbi algorithm for finding the most likely state sequences in a hidden Markov model (Bishop, 2010), a globally optimal path is determined by backtrack from the goal to the start after an exhaustive local search of forward paths.
evidence: This is a statement about computational algorithms.

claim: The model enables similar path finding mechanism through reverse replay.
source: Our model enables similar path finding mechanism through reverse replay.
evidence: This is a claim about the computational function of the model.

claim: Such a mechanism has been suggested in machine learning literature, but whether and how neural dynamics achieves it remained unknown.
source: Such a mechanism has been suggested in machine learning literature (Foster and Knierim, 2012), but whether and how neural dynamics achieves it remained unknown.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the neural implementation.

claim: The model predicts the roles of neuromodulators that modify plasticity rules and activity levels in sequence learning.
source: In addition, our model predicts the roles of neuromodulators that modify plasticity rules and activity levels in sequence learning.
evidence: This is a statement about predictions of the model.

claim: These predictions are testable by physiological experiments.
source: These predictions are testable by physiological experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the testability of the model's predictions.
